Funny Square

GeometryConstructionsCoordinates
What it shows: Three dots on one straight line build a four-sided shape that stays a square.
How to play: Drag the dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to see the construction lines or the matching triangles.
Look for the math

Drag a dot and the shape changes size and turns, yet its four sides stay equal and its corners stay right angles. This is the square the original page calls "from nowhere".

The three upright lines

The page's exact claim is that P and Q lie on AR with AP = QR, and that perpendicular lines at P, Q and R have PD = PR, QB = QR and RC = PQ. Then ABCD is a square. The logic test checks all six lengths and every corner across 672 configurations, including P and Q outside the segment and A and R the other way round. The claim holds in every one.

Why it always works

Write u = AP and v = PR as signed lengths, and take screen coordinates with y growing downward. Put A = (a, y), so P = (a+u, y), R = (a+u+v, y) and, because QR = u, Q = (a+v, y). The three perpendiculars end at

B = (a+v, y+u), D = (a+u, y−v), C = (a+u+v, y+u−v).

Now two vectors do all the work: AB = (v, u) and AD = (u, −v). Their dot product is uv − uv = 0, so the corner at A is a right angle, and both have length √(u² + v²). Also BC = AD and CD = −AB, so the shape is a square. The page says its triangle proof needs adjusting when the points fall outside AR; this vector proof does not, because signed lengths work there too.

A quirk in the old bytecode

A literal reading of the applet's Compute() gives Q.x = R.x − P.x − A.x. That agrees with AP = QR only when A.x = 0; at any other offset it draws a different quadrilateral. This port follows the page's stated construction instead, so the picture is a square wherever you drag the base line. The logic test transcribes the bytecode a second time, confirms it agrees with this core at the origin in 105 cases, and confirms that the bytecode's own default diagram fails the page's claim while this one passes.

Try dragging P past R, then tick Hint: the triangle BTC appears with BT running along the base and CT equal to PD.
